result.summary: You successfully identified the ocean floor mapping evidence and the mechanism of sea-floor spreading that revived continental drift. However, you lost credit by reversing the age of rocks at the ridge crest and the depth of earthquake foci at ridges and trenches. You should first correct the rock age sequence to show that the youngest rocks are at the crest.

result.question: How did the concept of sea-floor spreading revive the idea of continental drift and lead to the theory of plate tectonics? (Answer in 150 words)

sentences.text: Wegener's continental drift theory was largely rejected because the forces he proposed were considered inadequate.
Post-war mapping of the ocean floor supplied the missing evidence.
The surveys revealed mid-oceanic ridges marked by frequent volcanic eruptions.
Rocks nearest the crest of the ridges were found to be the oldest, with age decreasing away from the crest.
Rocks equidistant on either side of the crest were remarkably similar.
Oceanic crust proved far younger than continental rocks, and ocean-floor sediments were unexpectedly thin.
Earthquakes along the mid-oceanic ridges were found to be deep-seated, while those at the trenches had shallow foci.
From these facts Harry Hess proposed that magma erupting at the ridges pushes the crust apart, while older crust sinks and is consumed at the trenches.
McKenzie, Parker and Morgan then synthesised these ideas into plate tectonics, in which rigid lithospheric plates move over the asthenosphere, driven by mantle convection.
Plate tectonics now explains the distribution of earthquakes, volcanoes and fold mountains like the Himalayas, aiding seismic hazard mapping.
